extraction_text: King Janamejaya asks about the secret of Surya (Sun God) that was not told to Karna, and about Karna's earrings and armor.

attributes.action: Inquiry about divine secret and artifacts

extraction_text: A Brahmin appears before King Kuntibhoja, described as energetic, radiant, bearded, with matted hair, holding a staff, flawless in form, handsome, with honey-colored skin and sweet speech.
The Brahmin requests to live in King Kuntibhoja's house for food, with conditions that no one should neglect or offend him, and he can come and go as he pleases.
King Kuntibhoja agrees to the Brahmin's request and offers his daughter Pritha (Kunti) to serve the Brahmin respectfully.
King Kuntibhoja praises Pritha's character to the Brahmin, describing her as well-behaved, gentle, humble, respectful to all, and pleasing to everyone.
King Kuntibhoja reveals Pritha's origin: she was born in the Vrishni clan as the daughter of Sura, sister of Vasudeva, and given to Kuntibhoja as his eldest daughter.

attributes.true_identity: Pritha is Sura's daughter, Vasudeva's sister, adopted by Kuntibhoja

extraction_text: King Kuntibhoja advises his daughter Kunti (Pritha) to serve a Brahmin with devotion to avoid his wrath and bring happiness.

key_points: Kunti is praised for her noble birth and beauty
Warning about Brahmin's power to destroy if angered
Reference to Sage Mandavya's curse on King Nala due to Damayanti

extraction_text: Kunti promises King Kuntibhoja she will serve the Brahmin carefully and respectfully at all times.

key_points: Kunti vows to never anger the Brahmin
Acknowledges Brahmins' power to save or destroy
References Sage Mandavya's curse as cautionary example

extraction_text: King Kuntibhoja gives his daughter Kunti to the Brahmin for service.

key_points: King Kuntibhoja asks Brahmin to forgive any mistakes

extraction_text: King Kuntibhoja provides the Brahmin with a white, beautiful house.

supernatural_elements: House described as white like swans and moonlight

extraction_text: Princess Pritha (Kunti) diligently served the Brahmin in his fire-worship hall, arranging seats, food, and all necessities.

relationships: Pritha serves Brahmin with utmost respect

extraction_text: Pritha served the Brahmin wholeheartedly, abandoning laziness and pride, pleasing him as if serving a god.
Pritha maintained her service despite the Brahmin's unpredictable schedule, harsh words, and difficult demands.
King Kuntibhoja regularly asked his daughter if the Brahmin was satisfied with her service.
After one year of flawless service, the Brahmin offered Pritha a boon for her exceptional devotion.
Pritha initially declined the boon, saying her duty was already fulfilled.
The Brahmin insisted and gave Pritha a mantra that could summon and control any god.

relationships: Brahmin bestows powerful gift on Pritha
supernatural_elements: Mantra to summon and control gods

extraction_text: Pritha accepted the mantra, fearing to refuse the Brahmin's gift.

relationships: Pritha receives divine power from Brahmin

extraction_text: The Brahmin (Durvasa) tells King Kuntibhoja that he has been comfortable in his home and is satisfied with the girl (Kunti), then disappears.

attributes.relationships: Durvasa was a guest; Kunti served him well.

extraction_text: After some time, Kunti, curious about the mantra's power, finds herself menstruating and feels shy as an unmarried girl.
Kunti sees the sun rise, gains divine sight, and sees the deity Surya (the Sun God) in his divine form.
Kunti, out of curiosity, uses the mantra to summon Surya, who appears before her.
Surya explains that he is under Kunti's control due to the mantra and offers to serve her, but Kunti asks him to leave, apologizing for her curiosity.

attributes.relationships: Surya is compelled by the mantra; Kunti regrets the summoning.

extraction_text: Surya refuses to leave without consequence, stating that summoning a deity without purpose is inappropriate and threatens to curse Kunti, her father, and Durvasa if she does not accept union with him.

attributes.relationships: Surya asserts divine authority; Kunti is pressured.

extraction_text: Surya reveals that Kunti's true desire is to bear a son with him, who will be heroic and possess armor and earrings, and insists on union to avoid his wrath.

attributes.relationships: Surya interprets the summoning as a desire for progeny.

extraction_text: Surya notes that other gods, led by Indra, are watching and mocking him for being summoned by Kunti, and grants her divine sight to see them.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Kunti gains ability to see gods; divine mockery occurs.

extraction_text: Kunti sees the gods of the thirty-three heavens in their realms, with Surya shining brightly among them.
The young princess Kunti, upon seeing the Sun God, expressed fear and shame, asking him to leave and explaining that only her parents or elders could give her body away.

relationships: Kunti appeals to Sun God as a child seeking forgiveness

extraction_text: Sun God responded that he was treating her gently because she was a child, urged her to marry him voluntarily for happiness, and argued that returning after being summoned would make him a laughingstock among gods.

relationships: Sun God pressures Kunti to accept union
supernatural_elements: Sun God promises a son like himself if she consents

extraction_text: Kunti, unable to persuade Sun God and fearing his curse, worried about protecting her innocent father and brahmins from his wrath.

relationships: Kunti fears consequences for her family

extraction_text: Kunti, torn between fear of curse and concern for family reputation, proposed a conditional acceptance: if Sun God deemed it lawful, she would satisfy his wish while maintaining her chastity, appealing to him for protection of dharma, reputation, and life.

relationships: Kunti seeks Sun God's assurance for lawful union
supernatural_elements: Appeal to Sun God's authority over dharma and life

extraction_text: Sun God argued that neither parents nor elders could grant her happiness, interpreted the word 'kanya' (girl) as meaning 'free' and 'loving all', and assured her that no law would be broken.

relationships: Sun God asserts Kunti's freedom to choose
supernatural_elements: Divine interpretation of language and law

extraction_text: Sun God (Surya) proposes to Kunti (also called Pritha) that she will bear a son while remaining a virgin.
Kunti requests that her son have earrings and divine armor.

relationships: Mother-to-be making conditions for her son

extraction_text: Sun God agrees, promising earrings from Aditi and divine armor made of amrita (nectar).
Kunti agrees to the union with Sun God.
Sun God enters Kunti through yoga, touching her navel and impregnating her without violating her virginity.
Sun God departs after confirming Kunti will bear a heroic son and remain a virgin.
Kunti conceives and carries the fetus for ten fortnights, hiding her pregnancy from everyone except her nurse.
Kunti gives birth to a radiant son with golden earrings, divine armor, orange eyes, and bull-like shoulders resembling his father.
Kunti and her nurse decide to place the newborn in a sealed, cushioned basket and set it afloat on the Ashva River.

plot_points: Sets up Karna's future discovery and upbringing

extraction_text: Kunti, fearing her father's discovery of her illegitimate pregnancy, places her newborn son in a basket and sets it adrift in the Ashwa River while weeping and praying for his safety.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Kunti invokes numerous gods (Varuna, Vayu, Surya, Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sadhyas, Maruts, Indra) for protection. The infant is described as wearing divine armor and earrings born from nectar.

extraction_text: The basket drifts from the Ashwa River to the Charmanyavati River, then to the Yamuna River, and finally into the Ganga River.

attributes.relationships: The infant is alone in the basket.
attributes.supernatural_elements: The divine armor and earrings, along with fate, are said to preserve the infant.

extraction_text: In the Ganga River, the basket drifts to the Champa region in the country of Anga.

attributes.relationships: The infant arrives in a new land.
attributes.supernatural_elements: The infant travels on the waves.

extraction_text: A charioteer named Adhiratha, a friend of King Dhritarashtra, comes to the Ganga with his wife Radha, who is beautiful but childless and has been making great efforts to have a son.

extraction_text: Radha, by chance, discovers the drifting basket with a handle and amulets, which the waves of the Ganga push toward her. Out of curiosity, she seizes the basket and tells Adhiratha.

attributes.relationships: Radha finds the infant, setting the stage for adoption.
attributes.supernatural_elements: The basket is described as having amulets.

extraction_text: The charioteer Adhiratha (also called Ratha or Shantanu's charioteer in some versions, but here clearly Adhiratha) lifted a basket from the water and opened it with a tool, finding an infant inside.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Infant found in basket in water

extraction_text: The infant was radiant like the morning sun, wearing golden armor and earrings.

attributes.relationship: Adhiratha and Radha accept the infant as their son

extraction_text: Adhiratha gave the child to Radha, who accepted him with proper rituals.

attributes.relationship: Karna raised as Radha's son alongside her biological children

extraction_text: The valiant prince thus became the charioteer's son, known as Vasushena and also as Vrishasena.

In Hastinapura, Karna learned weapons from Drona, became friends with Duryodhana, and learned four types of warfare from Drona, Kripa, and Rama, becoming a famous archer.
